lesson.title: Counting Cognates Gym
lesson.subtitle: un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix, vingt — Latin roots in everyday counting.

hook.title: Every French Number Has an English Twin
hook.content: Every number 1 to 20 shares its Latin root with an English word you already know: un (unit), deux (duo/deuce), trois (trio), quatre (quartet), cinq (quintet), six (six), sept (September), huit (octopus/October), neuf (November), dix (decimal), vingt (vigesimal).

footnotes.title: How six, huit, and dix change their final sound by context
footnotes.content: Standing alone, six (/sis/) and dix (/dis/) end in /s/, and huit (/ɥit/) ends in /t/. Before a consonant (six jours, huit livres, dix minutes), their final consonant goes silent! Before a vowel (six‿ans, huit‿heures, dix‿euros), S/X buzzes as /z/ and T taps as /t/!

pattern.title: Count With Cognates and Watch Liaison Before Vowels
pattern.content: Practice pairing numbers with minutes, hours, euros, and days: cinq minutes, sept jours, huit heures, dix euros, vingt ans.
pattern.linguist_note: Sandhi alternation on six, huit, dix preserves three distinct historical environments.
pattern.trap_note: Don't pronounce the p of sept (/sɛt/) or the gt of vingt (/vɛ̃/) when standing alone!

exercises.prompt: Match each French number phrase with its meaning:
exercises.target_answer: two coffees, four people, five minutes, seven days, ten euros
exercises.meaning: deux cafés (duo), quatre personnes (quartet), cinq minutes (quintet), sept jours (September), dix euros (decimal)
exercises.explanation: Every number 1–10 connects to an English Latinate cognate.

exercises.prompt: French cinq ('five') shares its Latin root quinque with which English word for a five-musician group?
exercises.explanation: Latin quinque gave English quintet/quintessential and French cinq.

exercises.prompt: In 'sept jours' ('seven days'), which letter in 'sept' is completely silent?
exercises.meaning: The p of sept is always silent; the t is always pronounced (/sɛt/)!
exercises.explanation: Just like English 'receipt', the p in sept is an etymological ghost.

exercises.idea: I have five minutes and ten euros
cues: I have five minutes → J'ai cinq minutes
and ten euros → et dix euros
exercises.target_answer: J'ai cinq minutes et dix euros
exercises.meaning: I have five minutes and ten euros

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Nous avons sept jours à Paris
exercises.target_answer: Nous avons sept jours à Paris
exercises.meaning: We have seven days in Paris
exercises.affirmation: You wrote Nous avons sept jours à Paris cleanly.

summary.outcome: Count with 1–20 in real contexts and apply liaison on six, huit, dix, and vingt.

use_example.english: I've been waiting for five minutes.

summary.takeaway: Numbers 1–20 are Latin cognates you already own in English.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([1502] Four Score & Seven): see how Counting Cognates Gym leads directly into Four Score & Seven.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I have five minutes and ten euros" in French:
twist.target_answer: J'ai cinq minutes et dix euros
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "J'ai cinq minutes et dix euros" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Counting Cognates Gym.

deux.etymology_derivation: Latin duo — English duo, deuce (the two-card).

trois.etymology_derivation: Latin trēs and English three share the Proto-Indo-European *treyes — the oldest cognate pair on the trail.

quatre.etymology_derivation: Latin quattuor — quartet, quarter. And quatre-vingts is four twenties: the count of 'four score'.

cinq.etymology_derivation: Latin quinque — quintet, quintessence (the fifth element).

six.etymology_derivation: Final x sounds like /s/ alone, is silent before a consonant (six jours /si ʒuʁ/), and buzzes as /z/ before a vowel (six ans /si.z‿ɑ̃/).

sept.etymology_derivation: Latin septem — September was month seven of the old calendar before January butted in.

huit.shift_rule: Latin octō, o breathed into hu-
huit.etymology_derivation: Latin octō — octopus, October. French breathed an h in front: huit.

neuf.etymology_derivation: Latin novem 'nine' — November, the ninth month. The same word (from novus) also means new.

vingt.etymology_derivation: Latin vīgintī — English 'vigesimal' (counting by twenties) is the same root; French just kept counting that way: quatre-vingts.
